p.title: Image as Data: Automated Content Analysis for Visual Presentations of Political Actors and Events

ext.title: Image as Data: Automated Content Analysis for Visual Presentations of Political Actors and Events
ext.document_type: Journal article (open access, CC BY 4.0), with lettered appendices A-G and references. Metadata hint corrected: authors are Jungseock Joo (UCLA Communication) and Zachary C. Steinert-Threlkeld (UCLA Public Policy); the hint's title and year were correct; full DOI and page range added.
ext.coverage: Read all 2,595 lines of the extracted text (front matter through references and appendices A-G) and all 65 items in the annotation JSON. Page mapping: annotation "page" = PDF page; printed journal page = PDF page + 10. Covered text in the annotations is raw PDF extraction, so two-column lines are interleaved and some items are fragments; the trimmed covered text below is cut to roughly the first 25 words. Lobbying, network analysis, path-finding and resource allocation do not appear in the paper. Elections, persuasion and turnout appear only as literature background and in the vote-choice and mobilization claims (printed p.14-15). Text measurement appears only as contrast (Appendix A, printed p.36-38).
ext.research_question: Can large-scale image data be analyzed with deep learning / convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to measure political communication that text methods and small manual codings cannot reach? Two applied questions: (1) how U.S. politicians' Facebook photographs differ by party and gender, measured with an off-the-shelf label API; (2) how protest images shared on Twitter frame events, with testable expectations that protest images emphasize state violence over protester violence (H1) and crowds over individuals (H2).
ext.theory: Visual information is processed more easily and emotionally than text (Graber 1996; Grabe and Bucy 2009); the visual cue may dominate when visual and verbal cues conflict (Gibson and Zillmann 2000); images are information shortcuts for complex issues (Popkin 1994). Ideology predicts object emphasis (conservative: nationalism, capitalism; liberal: inequality reduction); gender predicts self-presentation of physical features (Carpinella et al. 2016; Bauer and Carpinella 2018). Protest framing: frames affect recruitment (Benford and Snow 2000); protester violence reduces support while state violence increases it, so protesters should emphasize state violence (H1); crowds lower individual risk and create mobilization feedback, so protesters should emphasize crowds (H2) (Moore 1995; Biggs 2016).
ext.identification: None causal. Study 1: descriptive chi-squared association between party (or gender-by-party) and label presence, no controls, no multiple-comparison correction reported. Study 2: descriptive comparison of duplication rates across events and labels, no inferential statistics; hypothesis check is by comparing rates within events (H1 state vs protester violence; H2 group vs child/faces).
ext.data: Study 1: 15,647 public Facebook photographs (timeline, mobile and profile albums, via the Graph API) posted by 677 candidates in the 2018 U.S. general election, Aug 5 to Nov 6, 2018. Unit = photograph (candidate-level sample; candidate list from Wikipedia, accounts identified manually). Each photo was sent to Google's Label Detection API; 1,730 unique labels were returned. Per-party and per-gender Ns are not stated in the main text. Study 2: geolocated tweets and their images from five protest episodes: Catalonia (Spain, secessionist, 2017), Hong Kong (2014, electoral reform), Russia (anti-corruption, 26 Mar 2017), South Korea (2016-17, Park Geun-hye), and Venezuela (2014-15), printed p.31-33 and footnote 5. Tweets were not keyword-filtered. The analysis sample N is not stated in the main text. Protest-image classifier training set: 32,611 images (Appendix D, printed p.48-50 and Fig. D1/D2 captions). Training images were a mixture of Google Image results and geolocated tweet images.
ext.method: Study 1: off-the-shelf Google Vision Label Detection (no training); label prevalence by party computed as the share of images with each label (pD, pR); chi-squared test per label, separate for male and female candidates; labels sorted by chi-square (Tables 1-2, printed p.28-29). Unsupervised check: ImageNet-pretrained CNN features (2,048-dim penultimate layer), k-means with k=200 (Appendix F, printed p.54-55). Study 2: fine-tuned ResNet-50 (He et al. 2016) for protest image classification and for violence/police/fire/sign labels; FairFace classifier (Karkkainen and Joo 2019) for face sex, race and age; six frame labels (contains child, faces, large group, small group, protester violence, state violence); duplicate detection via cosine-style pairwise distance on the 1,000-dim last fully connected layer, duplicate if normalized distance below 0.2 (threshold chosen by inspecting the histogram); framing rate = share of duplicate images within each event-label (Table 3, printed p.33). Background sections describe CNN architecture, transfer learning, training, validation (Grad-CAM visualization, Appendix D) and ethics. Table D1 compares architectures (AlexNet, VGG-16/19, ResNet-18/34/50) for protest fine-tuning.
ext.scope: Population: candidates in the 2018 U.S. general election (Facebook photos) and protest-related Twitter images from five protest episodes in Catalonia, Hong Kong, Russia, South Korea and Venezuela (2014-2017). Institutions: U.S. elections and social-media platforms. Era: 2014 to 2018 data, published 2022. The paper is a methods tutorial with two applications, so the external validity of the substantive findings is explicitly limited.

key_findings.finding: Among male candidates, Republicans' photographs over-index official and military/uniform labels; Democrats' over-index adaptation, community, youth and conversation labels. Top Republican-male labels: Official (chi2 53.0, pD 9.69%, pR 14.64%), Military officer (16.6; 1.02% vs 2.09%), Uniform (15.0; 2.50% vs 3.94%). Top Democratic-male labels: Adaptation (60.6; 6.87% vs 3.39%), Community (43.9; 28.81% vs 22.87%), Youth (30.8; 6.59% vs 4.05%).
key_findings.location: Section 6.1 and Table 1, printed p.28 (PDF p.18)
key_findings.numbers: chi2 53.0-60.6 for top labels; pD/pR shares given in Table 1

key_findings.finding: Female candidates show a weaker cross-party gap than male candidates (no military concepts among Republican women), but Republican women's photos carry traditional feminine labels. Top Republican-female labels: Red (chi2 59.8; pD 2.23%, pR 6.30%), Blond (51.1; 3.68% vs 8.21%), Jeans (42.7; 1.30% vs 4.01%), Long hair (8.0; 1.80% vs 3.03%), Pink (6.4; 2.46% vs 3.71%), Beauty (6.0; 1.64% vs 2.66%). Top Democratic-female labels: Glasses (41.6; 9.73% vs 4.51%), Adaptation (34.3; 7.12% vs 3.03%), Youth (27.2; 11.87% vs 7.16%).
key_findings.location: Table 2 (printed p.29, PDF p.19); discussion printed p.30
key_findings.numbers: chi2 41.6-59.8 for top labels; the authors say female candidates emphasize facial features more than males

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that politicians combine partisan values with gender stereotypes in their self-presentation (Bauer and Carpinella 2018).
Unsupervised k-means (k=200) on CNN features yields clusters of very similar or identical images, e.g. a cluster of John McCain photographs posted after his death on Aug 25, 2018.
key_findings.location: Printed p.30 and Appendix F p.54-55 (Fig. F1)

key_findings.finding: H1 partly supported: images containing state violence are shared more than protester violence in three of five events (Catalonia 0.304 vs 0.212; South Korea 0.042 vs 0.023; Venezuela 0.308 vs 0.280). Hong Kong (0.034 vs 0.047) and Russia (0.100 vs 0.121) go the other way.
key_findings.location: Table 3 (printed p.33, PDF p.23); text printed p.32-35
key_findings.numbers: framing = share of duplicate images per event-label

key_findings.finding: Venezuela has the highest framing intensity across all six labels. The most duplicated event-label, Venezuela state violence (0.308), is about 103 times the least, Hong Kong children (0.003). Rank order of labels correlates across events, which the authors read as a hierarchy of frames.
key_findings.location: Table 3 and text, printed p.34-35 (PDF p.24-25)

key_findings.finding: H2 partly supported: group labels (large or small group) are duplicated more than the child/faces labels within events. Images of groups are shared at higher rates in three events, though not the same three that frame state violence. Protests framed as state violence (Catalonia and Venezuela) also emphasize group nature.
key_findings.numbers: Venezuela large group 0.249, small group 0.267; Catalonia large group 0.122, small group 0.144

key_findings.finding: The protest-image classifier (fine-tuned ResNet-50) reaches best accuracy 91.79% with best loss 0.213. VGG-16 scores slightly higher (92.33%, loss 0.204). Training set: 32,611 images. Accuracy per frame label is not reported in the main text.
key_findings.location: Table D1 and Appendix D, printed p.48-50 (PDF p.38-40); Fig. D1 caption

key_findings.finding: Methods finding: pretrained CNNs and commercial APIs can be used without training data, but their labels inherit dataset bias and face-classification accuracy gaps; the authors cite darker-skinned females at 65% vs lighter-skinned males at 99% accuracy for commercial gender-classification APIs.
key_findings.numbers: 65% vs 99% accuracy (Buolamwini and Gebru 2018, as cited)

limitations: Authors call the Study 2 results provisional and say they are not a definitive answer (printed p.33, PDF p.23).
Study 2 discards temporal variation and does not consider city or country correlates of frame emphasis (printed p.34, PDF p.24).
Framing is operationalized only as percentage duplicated images; the authors suggest counts of tweets and more frames as alternatives (printed p.34).
Study 2 uses a duplicate threshold of 0.2 chosen by inspecting one histogram; no sensitivity analysis is reported (printed p.32).
Google's Vision API architecture and training data are not published; the authors recommend validating API labels against manual annotations (footnote 2, printed p.57).
Labels inherit model and data bias; Google's gender label for photographs in image search underrepresents women relative to occupational share, as cited (Lam et al. 2018) (printed p.23-24).
Pretrained classifiers and APIs have inferior customizability; custom concepts require new annotated training data (printed p.30).

Interpretability: deep models have millions of parameters; validation relies on accuracy metrics plus visualization (Grad-CAM), which the authors say does not explain how the model reaches its output (printed p.51-53).
Privacy and consent: face detection can identify protesters, so researchers should not release identifiable photographs and should seek IRB approval for social-media image studies (printed p.24).
The paper does not report accuracy of the six frame labels in the main text; the verification it cites (Appendix G) is Grad-CAM visualization only (printed p.56).
Study 1 reports no multiple-comparison correction across roughly 1,700 labels; significance stars are per-label chi-squared tests (Tables 1-2).

Internal inconsistencies in the text: the conclusion says the protest example 'analyzes six protests' (printed p.36) while the study covers five countries; the text reports 'a tie in Russia' for protester vs state violence (printed p.35), but Table 3 shows 0.121 (protester) vs 0.100 (state).
Study 1 covers one election cycle (2018) and one platform (Facebook); photo sets are candidate-level and per-party or per-gender N is not stated.

rel.summary_md:
Joo and Steinert-Threlkeld (CCR 2022) is a methods tutorial on treating images as data, with two applications. Study 1 sends 15,647 Facebook photos from 677 candidates in 2018 through Google's label API. It runs chi-squared tests of label against party separately by gender, because the parties' gender ratios differ. Republican men over-index labels like Official and Military officer. Republican women over-index Blond and Red. There is no correction for testing about 1,700 labels. Study 2 fine-tunes a ResNet-50 (91.79% accuracy) on protest images from five protest episodes. It defines framing as the share of near-duplicate images per event and frame label, where a duplicate is a normalized feature distance below 0.2, a threshold picked from one histogram. H1 (state violence shared more than protester violence) and H2 (crowds shared more than individuals) each hold in 3 of 5 events. The authors call the results provisional. There is no causal identification.

For Paul's systems, the paper matters in one place. fec/network/frame_alignment.py ports both instruments to text: near-duplicate press titles across members (3-word-shingle Jaccard >= 0.5), and chi-squared category and term association with party. Checking the code showed that the transfer breaks on the unit of analysis. Joo's sharer chooses the image. The text port reads cu_press_stance_tone.csv with no source filter, and 816 of its 2,388 rows are americascreditunions.org articles that are attributed to each member they mention. One ACU headline credited to many members therefore counts as members echoing one script. In a single-path recompute that is UNVERIFIED under DE-062, General CU duplication falls from 60.2% (n=442) to 5.2% (n=116), and CU Tax Status from 64.7% (n=190) to 38.1% (n=42), once only *.senate.gov and *.house.gov rows are kept. The output is a diagnostic, last written 2026-07-01. It reaches salience_shock only under `--intensity auto`, and the chain does not pass that flag.

bearings.paper_claim: Framing = share of duplicate images within each event-label, duplicate when normalized distance of 1,000-dim last-layer vectors < 0.2; Venezuela state violence 0.308 vs Hong Kong children 0.003 (~103x). The sharer chooses which image to post, so duplication measures sharers aligning on a frame.
bearings.paper_location: Section 6.2 and Table 3, printed p.32-35 (PDF p.22-25)
bearings.system_side: Ports the duplication rate to press titles: an item counts as aligned if another member's title in the same regex category has 3-gram shingle Jaccard >= 0.5. The input is the full cu_press_stance_tone.csv with no domain filter. 816 of 2,388 rows are americascreditunions.org articles attributed to each member they mention, so one ACU headline credited to N members scores as N members echoing one script. Single-path recompute (UNVERIFIED, DE-062; window = whole CSV, file dated 2026-06-30): General CU 60.2% of 442 items -> 5.2% of 116 own-domain items; CU Tax Status 64.7% of 190 -> 38.1% of 42; ACU-only rows alone 79.8% (General CU) and 72.3% (Tax).
bearings.code_ref: fec/network/frame_alignment.py:3-13 (Joo mapping docstring), :22-23 (SRC = full press CSV, no own-domain filter), :38-55 (cross-member duplication rate)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The method carries over only when the duplicated unit was chosen by the actor being scored, as Joo's sharers chose their images. In this system that means own-domain releases (*.senate.gov, *.house.gov), the same filter the press pillar already uses. Third-party syndication measures the author's reach, not member coordination. Joo's frames come from a trained classifier; here they are regex categories, and titles are short, so a 3-gram Jaccard threshold of 0.5 behaves differently from a CNN-feature distance.

bearings.paper_claim: The 0.2 duplicate threshold was chosen by inspecting one histogram, with no sensitivity analysis. Framing is operationalized only as percentage duplicated, and the authors suggest tweet counts and more frames as alternatives. They call the Study 2 results provisional.
bearings.system_side: Calls Jaccard >= 0.5 the 'analog' of Joo's 0.2 and inherits the same untested choice. There is no threshold sweep, and the only audit check is that rates fall in [0,1]. Echo clusters use the same 0.5 cut, with a minimum of 3 items.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies directly. Before any alignment figure is quoted, it needs a threshold sweep (for example 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7) on own-domain rows. The paper offers no validation of the threshold that the system could borrow.

bearings.paper_claim: Chi-squared tests of label against party are run separately for male and female candidates because the two parties have different gender ratios. Labels are sorted by chi-square, with per-label stars and no multiple-comparison correction across ~1,700 labels.
bearings.system_side: The party-framing block computes chi-squared of category and title terms against party, pooled across chamber and source domain, with no strata and no correction. Press coverage differs by party (D 92.5% vs R 87%) and chamber (Senate 83% vs House 96%), and 34% of rows are ACU-authored. The brain note quotes 'D to CU-Bank Dynamics (chi-square = 128)' with no stratum or window.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Joo's own design argues for stratifying on the known compositional fault line. Here the fault lines are chamber and author domain. Until the test is stratified, the chi-square figures should carry an UNSTRATIFIED label and be read as descriptive term lists, not party-framing findings.

bearings.paper_claim: Joo frames consistent frames as more effective only by citing Wouters & Walgrave (2017) on frame consistency and policy response. Their own Study 2 is descriptive and does not test whether higher duplication produces larger effects.
bearings.system_side: Under `--intensity auto`, campaign intensity = 0.5 + alignment, in [0.5, 1.5], drawn from frame_alignment.json, and the docstring cites 'our CU Tax Status at 65%'. The chain runs `salience_shock.py --advise` with the default intensity of 1.0, so the alignment input does not reach the production advisory.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 0.5 + alignment mapping has no estimate behind it in Joo, and the 65% input it cites is inflated by ACU syndication. If auto intensity is ever turned on, it needs the own-domain recompute first, and the mapping should be treated as uncalibrated owner judgment.

gaps_exposed: Frame alignment has no source-author filter. The press pillar's own-domain rule (*.senate.gov / *.house.gov) is not applied in frame_alignment.py, so ACU syndication is counted as member coordination.
There is no sensitivity sweep on the near-duplicate threshold (Jaccard 0.5) and no human check that flagged title pairs are actually the same message. Joo leaves the same gap with the 0.2 threshold.
frame_alignment.json was last written 2026-07-01 and frame_alignment.py is not in run_pipeline.py, so the artifact is stale relative to later press refreshes.
The party-framing chi-square has no strata (chamber, author domain) and no multiple-comparison correction.

There is no visual channel (member photos, floor video). Joo's pointer to Dietrich (2018), where physical aisle-crossing predicts vote polarization, is the kind of behavioral 'monitoring' measure the system lacks. Paul's 'Monitoring tool?' note sits beside that material. Nothing is built, and the paper gives no validity evidence for congressional targeting.
Joo recommends validating off-the-shelf model labels against manual annotation before use. The frame-alignment duplicates and categories have never had a gold check.
flags: DATA ARTIFACT (UNVERIFIED, DE-062; single path): the frame-alignment headline figures (CU Tax Status 65%, General CU 60%) are driven by 816 americascreditunions.org rows, 34% of the 2,388-row cu_press_stance_tone.csv. Own-domain recompute: General CU 5.2% (n=116), CU Tax Status 38.1% (n=42), Defense 13.9% (n=36). A second path must reproduce this before the brain note is corrected.

The brain note (2026-07-feature-influence-engine-internals-salience-sna-wave.md:38) quotes 65%/60%/12% and chi-square = 128 with no window, denominator or stratum. That breaks the rule that every figure names its window and denominator, and the pooled chi-square needs an UNSTRATIFIED label.

The component description says frame alignment 'feeds salience intensity (0.5 + alignment)'. In the code this happens only under `--intensity auto`; the chain runs salience_shock --advise at the default 1.0 (run_pipeline.py:186), so production does not use it.
The salience_shock.py:200 docstring cites 'our CU Tax Status at 65%' as evidence of a coordinated shop. That figure is the contaminated one.

No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021 (LDA) or D-025: the paper argues for neither cosponsorship-edge dropping nor per-edge volume normalization, and the system draws no access or closeness language from it.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's position names Joo's duplicate-rate frame alignment as the template, and the system did build exactly that port (fec/network/frame_alignment.py, docstring lines 3-17), so the note matches what is built. It is stale on two points. First, it assumes the port measures member coordination. In fact one-third of its input is ACU-authored syndication, and removing those rows collapses General CU alignment from 60% to 5% (UNVERIFIED). Second, the measure does not reach production: it is not in the chain, and salience intensity uses it only on a non-default flag. Both of Paul's annotation documents list this paper as a citation only, with no takeaway. The 'Monitoring tool?' sticky beside Section 3 (printed p.17), next to the highlighted Dietrich (2018) passage on video aisle-crossing, points toward a visual or behavioral monitoring channel the system does not have. The paper gives no evidence that such a channel would carry over to CU targeting.

related.why: Same author, and ingested in the same 2026-07-01 six-paper wave. It is the text and Twitter counterpart to this image tutorial, and both inform how the system treats social-media posts as measurement.

Paul's position on frame-alignment cites both. Malaterre infers shared-attention communities from text (press HCoI), while Joo measures shared frames by duplication. Both rest on press text and have the same source-author attribution exposure.
Salience_shock implements Noble & Turner's going-public model and takes its optional campaign intensity from Joo-style frame alignment (salience_shock.py:198-209).

Joo cites Dietrich's video-based measure of legislator behavior (2018), the passage beside Paul's 'Monitoring tool?' note. Dietrich 2019 is the audio counterpart, behind the system's display-only prosody channel.
Same 'X as data' tutorial genre for audio. It shares Joo's cautions on validating off-the-shelf models and on measurement artifacts in non-text channels.
